entries.caption: Does “her offspring” predict the virgin birth? Genesis never says this child has no human father. That interpretation comes from the later Gospel story.
Does Genesis predict Jesus defeating Satan? The serpent only becomes Satan in later Christian interpretation. Genesis itself describes conflict between humans and snakes.
Is Enoch’s disappearance a preview of Jesus’s ascension? Enoch avoids death; Jesus dies and rises first. The stories have a resemblance, but also a crucial difference.
Did Noah predict that God would join Shem’s family? He calls the LORD “the God of Shem.” Turning that into a prediction about Jesus adds far more than the verse says.
Did God’s promise to bless the nations through Abraham predict Jesus? Paul reads it that way, but Genesis speaks about Abraham and does not identify a future individual.
Does the singular word “offspring” identify Jesus? In Genesis, the same word describes descendants as numerous as the stars. Singular grammar does not make it one person.
Does Melchizedek’s priesthood predict Jesus? Genesis supplies a striking comparison, but the actual promise of a future priest appears later, in Psalm 110.
Do Melchizedek’s titles predict Jesus? “King of righteousness” and “king of peace” describe Melchizedek himself. Hebrews makes the comparison much later.
Does Melchizedek’s bread and wine predict the Last Supper? It is a natural Christian symbol—but Genesis calls it neither a sacrifice nor a prediction.
Does God’s promise to Isaac identify Jesus? Jesus belongs to Isaac’s family, but so do countless others. The passage promises a lineage, not one particular descendant.
Did Abraham predict Jesus as God’s lamb? The story answers its own question: God provides a ram for Isaac’s sacrifice. Connecting that ram with Jesus comes later.
Does Abraham’s “offspring” mean one future saviour? Genesis also compares that offspring to countless stars. Acts and Paul focus the promise on Jesus later.
Did God promise a rescuer through Isaac? Genesis promises Isaac land, descendants and worldwide blessing. It never identifies one future Messiah.
Is Jesus Jacob’s ladder? Jesus reuses the image of angels ascending and descending, but Jacob’s dream is about God protecting Jacob—not predicting another person.
Does Jacob’s family line predict Jesus? Jesus is one of Jacob’s many descendants. An ancestry shared with countless people cannot identify him by itself.
Did Genesis reveal when Jesus would come? The disputed word “Shiloh” and an undefined royal deadline cannot provide a clear date for the Messiah.
Was Jesus promised through Judah? The passage points towards rule from Judah, and Jesus has the right ancestry. But a large family line cannot identify one person.
Was the name “Shiloh” a title for Jesus? The Hebrew is difficult, “the one sent” is not a secure translation, and John never calls Jesus Shiloh.
Did Jesus have to arrive before Judah disappeared? Genesis speaks about royal rule, not the tribe losing its identity. The supposed deadline is not in the text.
Does one flock under Jesus fulfil the nations obeying Judah’s ruler? The images are similar, but John never connects them. Resemblance alone does not establish prediction.
When Jesus says “I am,” is he using God’s name? Perhaps—but Exodus reveals God’s identity to Moses. It does not predict a future saviour.
Does the spotless Passover animal predict Jesus? The comparison works as Christian symbolism, but an ordinary ritual rule shared by other sacrifices is not a unique prediction.
Does Passover blood predict salvation through Jesus? Both stories involve rescue, but Exodus describes protection from a plague—not forgiveness of sins.
Paul explicitly calls Jesus “our Passover lamb.” The Christian comparison is undeniable. But that does not mean the original Exodus story was predicting him.
John says Jesus’s unbroken bones fulfil Scripture. The match is exact—but Exodus gives instructions for preparing a Passover meal, not a prediction of the Messiah’s death.
Is Jesus’s name hidden in the Hebrew word for “salvation”? The words are related, but Exodus uses an ordinary noun. It is not naming a future person.
Does God’s holiness in Exodus predict Jesus? Christians believe Jesus shares God’s character, but this song praises God for a past rescue. It predicts nobody.
Paul says the rock in the wilderness “was Christ.” That is an explicit Christian rereading—but Exodus itself describes emergency water, not a future saviour.
Does God’s mercy in Exodus predict Jesus’s mercy? Both passages describe God being merciful. Sharing a quality is not the same as making a prediction.
Does the “pleasing aroma” of sacrifice predict Jesus? Leviticus uses the phrase for many repeated offerings. Ephesians later applies the familiar image to Jesus.
